outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles the conjecture, moves its published verified range, or decides any case of its universal claim by proof: the post-freeze items are a 2025 journal paper giving heuristic support only, a 2024 Mersenne prime that adds one exponent satisfying condition B with condition C untested, and a 2026 preprint proving three Wagstaff numbers prime, which are instances only; no AI system is credited with any of it.
problem_asks: Let p range over all odd natural numbers. Write A for 'p = 2ᵏ ± 1 or p = 4ᵏ ± 3 for some natural number k', B for '2ᵖ − 1 is prime', and C for '(2ᵖ + 1)/3 is prime'. The statement asks for three implications, each for every odd natural p: (i) A and B imply C; (ii) A and C imply B; (iii) B and C imply A. Equivalently, no odd natural p satisfies exactly two of A, B, C. Composite odd p are covered automatically, since B and C both fail for them, so the content lies in the prime p. Nothing else is asked; the conjecture is not a bound or a classification.

events.what_happened: Paul T. Bateman, John L. Selfridge and Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr. state the 'new Mersenne conjecture' (the three-condition statement for odd p) in The American Mathematical Monthly, vol. 96 no. 2 (Feb. 1989), pp. 125-128, as an 'Editor's Corner' column (JSTOR stable 2323195, DOI 10.2307/2323195). It is a statement, not a proof. It was motivated by a statement Mersenne made in 1644, which is false, and by Lucas's later reading of it. The authors expected that no p > 127 satisfies all three conditions; the Wikipedia 'Mersenne conjectures' page quotes this expectation.
events.delivers: Nothing proved. Formulates the statement for all odd natural p and gives only a heuristic expectation: no p > 127 satisfies all three conditions. The known triples are 3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 31, 61, 127 (per the Wikipedia pages fetched, which give this as the current state).
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the three implications for every odd p.

checked_by.who: The American Mathematical Monthly, Editor's Corner column
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the note. The note is an editorial column, not a refereed proof, and it claims no proof.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the statement with the heuristic expectation.

events.time_since_posted: 37 years; no proof or refutation found since
events.directly_checkable: Any p can be tested by primality tests on 2ᵖ − 1 and (2ᵖ + 1)/3. That is how the verified ranges below were produced. The statement itself is a claim over all odd p, so a finite table is not a check of it.
events.doubts: Selfridge is reported to have called the conjecture 'a minor curious coincidence' and, per Silverman's account, 'obviously true' because it was chosen to fit known data. MathWorld and a 2005 mersenneforum thread (R. D. Silverman) tie it to Guy's Strong Law of Small Numbers, and an Ewmayer post in the same thread questioned whether it should be conjectured at all. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mersenne conjectures' (fetched, quotes Silverman's account); MathWorld (fetched); mersenneforum showpost p=53533 (fetched, April 2005).
events.direction: Not a result. It conjectures that no odd p satisfies exactly two of A, B, C. It does not assert that a counterexample exists or does not.

events.what_happened: Prime Puzzles' table for the conjecture attributes primality proofs of (2ᵖ + 1)/3 for several table exponents, including p = 10501, 12391 and 42737 and 'others', to François Morain, cited as [Morain1990a]. Entries for p = 11279 and 5807 (Mihailescu) and p = 10691 and 14479 (Broadhurst, via Primo) are also listed, with no dates. I did not open Morain's own text; the attribution comes only from the Prime Puzzles page.
events.delivers: Settles the condition-C question (is (2ᵖ + 1)/3 prime) for the listed exponents only. It is a set of instances; it does not touch the universal claim.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, and condition C for every other exponent.

checked_by.qualification: Author of the ECPP method used; cited on the Prime Puzzles table for these proofs
checked_by.what_they_did: Elliptic-curve primality proofs of (2ᵖ + 1)/3 for the listed exponents, as cited by Prime Puzzles

machine_checked.system: ECPP (elliptic-curve primality proving), as cited; not a Lean or Coq check

events.directly_checkable: Each listed exponent can be re-proved with an ECPP tool; I did not do so.
events.direction: Condition C is settled as true or false at each listed exponent. None of the listed cases produces a counterexample to the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Nuutti Kuosa reports on 10 February 2000 that (2^1048573 + 1)/3 is composite, using PRIMEFORM (a 315,652-digit number, 4-5 days on a PIII 450). This settles the pending case p = 1048573 that the Prime Puzzles table named as the smallest open exponent. Greg Childers confirmed the composite result with pfgw on 6 July 2001, obtaining the same residue (CBE3FC22FAE27F6) from two FFT runs. Yves Gallot's undated note says a verification is needed to rule out machine or code error.
events.delivers: Instance only. p = 1048573 = 4¹⁰ − 3, so A holds; B fails, since 1048573 is not in the GIMPS exponent list; C fails. Exactly one condition holds, which is consistent with the conjecture. This removes one pending entry from the table; it says nothing about other p.

checked_by.qualification: Independent computational check with pfgw on the same number
checked_by.what_they_did: Reran the compositeness test with pfgw and reported matching residues (6 July 2001)

events.directly_checkable: The verdict is a PRP/compositeness test result (PRIMEFORM, pfgw); no explicit factor is given. The residues recorded on the page are the only check.
events.doubts: The verdict rests on a computer test whose code or hardware error Yves Gallot flagged as needing verification. Pfgw reproduction by Childers is the only independent check recorded.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture at this p (exactly one of A, B, C holds). No counterexample.
events.object: A compositeness verdict for (2^1048573 + 1)/3, a number of 315,652 digits. It is not constructive: no factor is given.

events.what_happened: Henri Lifchitz reports that (2^1398269 + 1)/3 is composite. Greg Childers confirms the result with pfgw on 27 August 2001 (residue 183821950F064BF7, on a 1.2 GHz Athlon). The Prime Puzzles table lists p = 1398269 as a pending exponent; the page does not date Lifchitz's original post, so 27 August 2001 is the earliest dated mention found.
events.delivers: Instance only. At p = 1398269, B holds (the GIMPS list gives 1398269 as the 35th Mersenne prime exponent, found 1996), A fails (1398269 is neither 2ᵏ ± 1 nor 4ᵏ ± 3), and C fails. Exactly one condition holds, which is consistent with the conjecture. It settles only this exponent.

checked_by.what_they_did: Confirmed the composite result and residue (27 August 2001)

events.directly_checkable: A pfgw compositeness verdict with a recorded residue; no factor is given.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture at this p. No counterexample.
events.object: A compositeness verdict for (2^1398269 + 1)/3, with residue 183821950F064BF7. It is not constructive: no factor is given.

events.what_happened: Richard Chen posts on 21 June 2021 (on the Prime Puzzles conjecture page, which Caldwell's Prime Pages NMC page cites) that the conjecture 'has been verified for all primes p <= 1073741826'. Neither the method nor the code is published in any source I read. The Prime Puzzles page also has a status table for small p.
events.delivers: A finite-range computational claim: every prime p up to 1073741826 satisfies the conjecture, per the poster. It covers finitely many p. The statement is universal over all odd p, so this does not move any quantity the statement names beyond the bound itself.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for p above 1073741826, and the universal claim for all p.
events.directly_checkable: Each p can be rechecked by primality tests on 2ᵖ − 1 and (2ᵖ + 1)/3. No code or method was published that I could find.
events.doubts: A forum-style posting with no published method, code, or independent recheck. The bound is quoted differently across sources: Prime Pages' page cites 10,000,000 (via Wikipedia's current text); MathWorld cites 12,441,900 with no source; Wikipedia's current text states 'less than 1073741827' for the first condition, without naming Chen. These are the sources I read.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture up to the bound. No counterexample reported.

events.what_happened: GIMPS announces (press release datelined Blowing Rock, NC, 21 October 2024) the 52nd Mersenne prime, 2^136279841 − 1 (41,024,320 decimal digits). Luke Durant found it on 12 October 2024; the Lucas-Lehmer test confirmed it; official credit reads 'L. Durant, M. Preda, G. Woltman, A. Blosser, et al.' Wikipedia's list marks rank 52 and above as provisional. Press coverage mentions GPUs; GPUs are computing hardware, not AI.
events.delivers: A new instance of condition B: 2^136279841 − 1 is prime. Exponent 136279841 is not of the form 2ᵏ ± 1 or 4ᵏ ± 3 for any k (checked by hand), so A fails. The conjecture therefore predicts that (2^136279841 + 1)/3 is composite; a prime value would be a counterexample. Nothing in this event tests C. It does not move the verified range: Wikipedia's current text says the Mersenne exponent list is complete only up to 82,589,933, and 136279841 lies beyond that.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including condition C at p = 136279841, which I found no report of anyone testing.

checked_by.who: GIMPS (Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search) verification process
checked_by.qualification: The project that runs and double-checks Lucas-Lehmer tests for Mersenne numbers
checked_by.what_they_did: Lucas-Lehmer primality test confirmed the number; announced in the press release

events.directly_checkable: Yes for condition B: the Lucas-Lehmer test on 2^136279841 − 1. Condition C at this exponent would need a probable-prime or ECPP test on a 41-million-digit number, and I found no report of one.
events.direction: Instance of condition B only. The conjecture predicts C fails here. No counterexample found, and none is possible from B alone.
events.object: The Mersenne prime 2^136279841 − 1 (41,024,320 digits). By itself it is not a counterexample: it becomes one only if (2^136279841 + 1)/3 is also prime.

events.what_happened: Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr., 'Two Mersenne Prime Conjectures', Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.2. The abstract reads: 'We discuss two conjectures about Mersenne numbers, an old one and a new one. Heuristic arguments support both conjectures.' The PDF outline lists the sections 'Introduction', 'The 1989 New Mersenne Conjecture', 'Chen's Mersenne Conjecture of 2025' and 'Acknowledgements'. The full PDF was not readable with my tools, so the heuristic details and the 2025 Chen conjecture's statement are unverified. Search excerpts (not opened text) describe the heuristic as treating the three exponent sets as exponentially growing sequences whose overlap is expected to be empty or finite, and predicting that no p > 127 satisfies two of the conditions.
events.revisions: Received 1 Sep 2025; revised 27 Sep 2025; published 4 Dec 2025 (journal abstract page). No arXiv or other version found.
events.delivers: Heuristic support for the 1989 conjecture; the abstract claims no proof and no new verified range. Per search excerpts only (not verified): a heuristic model of the three exponent sets; the paper also says that the 1989 conjecture holds in the range of all known Mersenne primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the conjecture is unproven. The 2025 'Chen' conjecture discussed in the same paper is a different conjecture and is not established as bearing on this one.

checked_by.who: Journal of Integer Sequences (refereed editorial process)
checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed number-theory journal. The received and revised dates imply refereeing, but the page does not state it.
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper on 4 December 2025

events.doubts: The abstract says the support is heuristic. The author co-proposed the 1989 conjecture, so this paper is not an independent reading of it. I found no published response, verification, or dispute of the paper.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture heuristically. Gives no counterexample and claims no proof.

events.what_happened: Alexey Dolotov, 'Three Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge primality proofs for Wagstaff numbers', arXiv:2605.18555 (submitted 18 May 2026, math.NT, one version). It gives unconditional primality proofs of W_p = (2^p + 1)/3 at p = 2617, 10501 and 12391, using the Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge N-1 criterion on the cyclotomic factorisation of 2^(p-1) - 1, with code and certificates on Zenodo. The abstract does not mention the New Mersenne conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 only, as of my fetch
events.delivers: Condition C is established as true at p = 2617, 10501 and 12391. For these three exponents A and B both fail (none of them is of the form 2ᵏ ± 1 or 4ᵏ ± 3, and none is a Mersenne exponent), so exactly one condition holds and the conjecture is consistent. The result is three instances of C.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, and condition C at every other exponent.
events.directly_checkable: Yes in principle: the certificates on Zenodo, which I did not download or check.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture at three exponents. No counterexample.
events.object: Primality certificates for W_2617 (788 digits), W_10501 (3161 digits) and W_12391 (3730 digits), built by BLS N-1 on the cyclotomic factorisation of 2^(p-1) - 1.

summary: The conjecture (Bateman, Selfridge and Wagstaff, 1989, Amer. Math. Monthly, Feb. 1989, pp. 125-128) is unproven. Nothing since 26 January 2024 proves it, refutes it, decides a case of its universal claim by proof, or changes the verified range I could trace to a dated source. That range is p <= 1073741826, posted by Richard Chen on 21 June 2021 (Prime Puzzles, reproduced on Caldwell's Prime Pages page); I found no later range. The sources disagree on the range: Prime Pages, as quoted by Wikipedia, gives 10,000,000; MathWorld gives 12,441,900 with no source; and a figure of 30,402,456 attributed to 'Renaud Lifchitz' appeared only in search-result summaries, which I could not trace to any source, so I treat it as unverified (it may be a confusion with Henri Lifchitz's 2001 composite result). The pending exponents on the Prime Puzzles table were p = 1048573 and p = 1398269; both were settled composite in 2000 and 2001 (Kuosa, Lifchitz, with pfgw confirmation by Childers), and both are consistent with the conjecture. Post-freeze events: (a) the 52nd Mersenne prime, 2^136279841 - 1, announced by GIMPS on 21 October 2024, which is an instance of condition B for an exponent where condition A fails, so the conjecture predicts that (2^136279841 + 1)/3 is composite; I found no report that this was tested, and Wikipedia's 2026 exponent-completeness line stops at 82,589,933; (b) Wagstaff's 'Two Mersenne Prime Conjectures' (J. Integer Sequences 28 (2025), 25.7.2, published 4 December 2025), whose abstract says only that heuristic arguments support both the 1989 conjecture and a 2025 'Chen' conjecture; I could not read the full PDF, so its heuristic details and the 2025 Chen statement are unverified (search excerpts attribute to Wagstaff the claim that no p > 127 satisfies two conditions, and a 'Chen's Conjecture 2' about the smallest Mersenne prime congruent to 1 mod p; I did not verify either); (c) Dolotov's 18 May 2026 preprint proving W_2617, W_10501 and W_12391 prime, which is three instances of condition C and does not mention the conjecture in its abstract. Close calls, written both ways: (1) the 2021 bound and the 2025 heuristic are finite or heuristic, so they move no quantity the statement names, which is how I read them; a reader who treats the verified range as the quantity could count the 2021 bound as the most significant movement since 1989. (2) Dolotov's proofs settle the primality of (2^p + 1)/3 at three exponents, which the statement treats as a case, not a settlement; Morain's 1990 ECPP proofs (cited by Prime Puzzles, primary text not opened) cover some of the same exponents, so Dolotov is not a new case for those. Silverman's 2005 report that Selfridge called it a 'minor curious coincidence', and Ewmayer's 2005 doubt, predate the window and are recorded under the 1989 event. On AI: no source names an AI system for this conjecture or its verified ranges. Searches covered the conjecture's name with AI terms and model names, the DeepMind formal-conjectures repository (not searchable: GitHub code search needs a login, and a gh code search was denied), the Epoch/OEIS-Open benchmark (read in full; the models it names, Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, resolve no Mersenne or Wagstaff entry among its visible results), AlphaEvolve's 67 problems (abstract only; no Mersenne problem named), and Sra's 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' (abstract only; no Mersenne mention). none_found is set true because no source I read names a system; the full texts of the 2025 and 2026 papers, including their acknowledgements, were not readable to me, so that flag is unverified for those two events. Bibliographic dating: the fetched Wikipedia pages give 1989 for the Monthly paper, and one search summary gave 1987 for Wikipedia's reference list; I did not see 1987 on the page itself.
competing_reading: The strongest case for counting something as progress is the 2021 verified range: Chen's bound (1073741826) is the largest published range and sits above Prime Pages' older figure, so a reader could treat it as a bound moved since the 1989 statement, and the 2025 heuristic paper as a new source of support. The case against is that a verified range is finitely many instances of a universal claim, and a heuristic is not evidence of a proof; the record leaves that weighing to the judging pass. A second reading counts Dolotov's three proofs as a settled case of condition C; the case against is that each is an instance, not a resolution, and the statement is about all odd p.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Wagstaff, J. Integer Sequences 28 (2025) 25.7.2 (wag14.pdf): the exact heuristic, the 2025 Chen conjecture's statement, and the acknowledgements, which would settle the AI question for that paper. (2) Richard Chen's 2021 method and code, or an independent rerun to 1073741826. (3) Whether (2^136279841 + 1)/3 has been tested for primality or compositeness, from the Prime Pages Wagstaff or NMC status pages, PrimeGrid, or the Cunningham pages. (4) The current Prime Pages, Lifchitz and Curry status pages, to reconcile 10,000,000, 12,441,900, 1,073,741,826 and the unsourced 30,402,456. (5) A search of google-deepmind/formal-conjectures for 'Mersenne' or 'Wagstaff' with an authenticated GitHub session. (6) The OEIS-Open per-A-number status of A107360 and A000978.
